text: the former Soviet Union, specifically Russia and Ukraine. In the opening days of the war, the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: conventional wisdom, and there's nothing wrong with that. But now that we're five weeks in, we're seeing a

text: much more nuanced picture with a lot of unexpected upsides and downsides for both sides. Let's start

text: It's conservatively removing a million and a half

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: they're just going to turn those drones under the next oil producing and transiting system. And we may not have any meaningful Russian exports from either the Baltic or the Black Sea within three months. We're that close.

text: Second, Ukraine itself. The year that the Ukrainians have had to basically operate without American assistance, they've used to great effect in innovating into the drone space, specifically in counter drone technology. They've got something called the Brave One, which can fit into a duffel bag and has limited range, not a great success rate, maybe 50%, but it only costs $2,000 to $3,000 to make versus $30,000 to $50,000

text: for a Shahed versus $4,000 for a Pac-3. So Zelensky in the last couple of weeks has been all over the Persian Gulf signing deals specifically with Kuwait and Qatar and the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, each multi-billion dollar deals to invest in drone production.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So we're going to be seeing money pouring into these facilities in Ukraine, which is going to drastically increase the defense of Ukraine from the Russians.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: At the same time, they'll be exporting drones to the Gulf states and the Gulf states will be building their own counter drone factories.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So we're talking about a whole number of countries that five years ago, no one really considered to be at the forefront of military tech.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: All of a sudden, at the forefront of military tech in a way that the United States can't participate in and isn't benefiting from.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So we've seen Ukraine and Russia get weird ups and downs in ways that were completely unexpected just a few weeks ago.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But perhaps the biggest impact of this is because the Russians are so actively assisting the Iranians,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: is that all of the Arabs of the Persian Gulf are noodling over what's next for them vis-a-vis the Russians and the United States.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And if you remember back to roughly 1985, when Reagan really started pushing hard on the Soviet Union,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: that was the year that the Saudis decided to drastically open up oil production in order to flood the market and bankrupt what was then the Soviet Union.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We now have the beginnings of a second generation of some sort of alliance like that.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But instead of the United States, it's the Europeans.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Instead of NATO, it's Ukraine.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And so we've got a number of pieces moving here, building new geopolitical alignments that really look very, very bad long term for Russia.

text: None of this I probably would have guessed at two months ago, but here we are.
